S065.name: Obsessions
S065.description: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, and attempts to ignore or suppress them.

subtypes.Contamination Obsessions: Recurrent and intrusive worries about contamination, germs, or dirt.
subtypes.Pathological Doubt: Pathological doubt regarding safety or mistakes, such as whether doors are locked or gas valves are closed.
subtypes.Symmetry and Exactness Obsessions: A strong urge that items must be lined up exactly or be symmetrical.
subtypes.Forbidden or Taboo Thoughts: Intrusive thoughts involving aggressive (harming others), sexual, or religious content that are prohibited.
subtypes.Somatic Obsessions: Persistent and specific fear that one might have a serious disease.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.

subtypes.Cleaning or Washing Compulsions: Repetitive acts to remove contamination, such as hand washing, showering, or excessive cleaning.
subtypes.Checking Compulsions: Repeatedly checking items like door locks, gas stoves, or switches to prevent danger.
subtypes.Ordering and Arranging Compulsions: Organizing objects in a specific order or at a precise angle to reduce anxiety.
subtypes.Mental Acts: Mental rituals performed internally, such as praying, counting, or repeating specific words silently.
subtypes.Repeating Rituals: Repeating specific actions (e.g., standing up, passing through a door) a set number of times.

symptom.disease_info: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is characterized by the presence of obsessions (intrusive, unwanted thoughts, images, or urges) and/or compulsions (repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed to reduce distress or prevent a feared event), which are time-consuming or cause significant distress or impairment. Onset is typically in adolescence or early adulthood and the course is usually chronic, with symptoms waxing and waning in response to stress; many patients have partial insight, recognizing their thoughts and behaviors as excessive. OCD is distinguished from anxiety disorders and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder by the ego-dystonic, intrusive quality of the thoughts and the ritualistic, often clearly irrational behaviors aimed at neutralizing them. It can be exacerbated by life stressors, high-responsibility roles, or environments that reward perfectionism and hypervigilance, and is frequently comorbid with depression and other anxiety disorders.

patient.personality: Patricia is meticulous, hyper-organized, and observant, balancing a disciplined, safety-focused mindset with a reflective, artistic side and a strong sense of responsibility toward others.
patient.stressor: Patricia’s problems intensified after she was promoted to a de facto lead role on the night shift in the casino surveillance room, following an incident in which a colleague missed a cheating scheme and the entire team was reprimanded. Already proud of her ability to catch tiny irregularities on CCTV, she began to feel personally accountable for preventing every possible theft, altercation, or self-harm event on the floor, especially during understaffed overnight shifts when she knew fewer eyes were on the monitors. Gradually, her work habits shifted from careful monitoring to elaborate, rigid routines of re-watching footage and double- or triple-documenting minor events before she could allow herself to move on, routines that spilled over into her home life as she created similar repetitive rituals around locks, appliances, and even her art supplies. She sought psychiatric help only after her exhaustion and lateness from extended end-of-shift “just one more check” cycles put her promotion at risk and her spouse expressed alarm that their evenings had become dominated by her need to repeatedly perform specific actions before she could sit down or go to bed.
patient.chief_complaint: “I feel like I have to keep doing the same things over and over, at work and at home, or I get so anxious that I can’t relax or move on.”

S065.name: Obsessions
S065.description: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, and attempts to ignore or suppress them.
S065.manifestation: It feels like my brain is constantly ambushing me with “what if” scenarios—like what if I missed someone slipping something into a drink on camera, or what if I actually left the front door unlocked and someone hurts my wife—over and over, no matter how many times I tell myself I already checked and it was fine.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.
S066.manifestation: Because of that, I end up stuck in these ridiculous routines, like rewinding the same footage three or four times before I let myself log an incident, or at home touching each lock and stove knob in a specific order and counting to eight in my head, and if anything feels off I have to start all over again or the anxiety just spikes through the roof.
